Puzzle 25 · 26 of 26

Why does every run load the same classes again?

Puzzles 11 and 17 showed HotSpot reading, parsing and linking each class the first time it's needed, and puzzles 19 to 24 showed every run warming up from nothing. Measure what a small Kotlin program spends on that at each start, and how much an archive prepared by an earlier run saves.

  • Puzzle 24: How long does score really take?

    A timing taken while code is still interpreted or at a lower level measures warm-up, and a timing of code whose result is unused can measure nothing at all, because C2 removes code whose result nobody reads. JMH warms the code up first, keeps every result alive, and runs each benchmark in a fresh JVM, so its number describes the compiled code you wanted to measure.

The problem

Puzzle 11 said a class is loaded, linked and initialized the first time code needs it, and puzzle 17 that its metadata is built in metaspace. A JVM does all of that again in every run, for the same classes, and then warms up again (puzzle 24). For a server that runs for weeks it hardly matters. For a command-line tool, a test run, or a container that is started for each request, startup is most of the run.

This Kotlin program sorts three bookmarks; kotlinc packed it and the Kotlin standard library into start.jar:

data class Bookmark(val url: String, val visits: Int)

fun main() {
    val bookmarks = listOf(Bookmark("a.dev", 3), Bookmark("b.dev", 7), Bookmark("c.dev", 1))
    val top = bookmarks.sortedByDescending { it.visits }.map { it.url }
    println(top.joinToString())
}

The -Xlog:class+load option prints one line per loaded class and says where it came from:

$ java -Xlog:class+load -jar start.jar
…
[0.034s][info][class,load] StartKt source: file:/…/start.jar
[0.034s][info][class,load] Bookmark source: file:/…/start.jar
…

Counting the lines: 597 classes came from a source called "shared objects file", and 41 from start.jar. With the -Xshare:off option, all 681 loaded classes came from class files. What is the shared objects file, and what does it save?

See it

The building block

Loading a class from a class file means reading its bytes from a jar, parsing them, and building the class's metadata in metaspace, before linking (puzzles 11 and 17). The result is the same in every run of the same program. Class data sharing (CDS) skips that work: HotSpot maps a prepared archive file into memory, and the classes in it are already in the form HotSpot keeps them. That file is a CDS archive. JEP 310: classes are "pre-processed into a shared archive file that can then be memory-mapped at runtime to reduce startup time".

Since JDK 12 the JDK ships one (JEP 341): the java manual says it "contains about 1300 core library classes that are used by most applications", in lib/server/classes.jsa. That's the "shared objects file" the 597 classes came from. Your own classes and the Kotlin library aren't in it: those 41 still come from the jar.

You can archive them too. Run the program once with ArchiveClassesAtExit; when it exits, HotSpot writes every class it loaded that isn't in the JDK's archive into a new one (JEP 350, JDK 13). That run is a training run: a run whose only purpose is to record what a later archive should contain.

$ java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -jar start.jar
b.dev, a.dev, c.dev
$ java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -Xlog:class+load -jar start.jar
…
[0.035s][info][class,load] StartKt source: shared objects file (top)
[0.035s][info][class,load] Bookmark source: shared objects file (top)
…

All 635 loaded classes now came from archives, none from the jar; (top) marks the app's archive, which sits on top of the JDK's. The time to start, run and exit, as the median of 21 runs, in two rounds:

RunClasses from class filesRound 1Round 2
-Xshare:off68195 ms97 ms
default (JDK's archive)4175 ms67 ms
SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa045 ms47 ms

Half the startup time of this program was loading classes. The rest, interpreting and warming up, an archive of classes doesn't touch. That's what the newer AOT cache goes after. JDK 24 (JEP 483) introduced it: an archive that stores classes "in a loaded and linked state", created from a training run in two steps:

java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -cp app.jar com.example.App
java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar
java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App

JDK 25 made it one step (JEP 514, with the AOTCacheOutput option) and added the method profiles from the training run (JEP 515), so that C2 can start "immediately upon application startup, rather than having to wait for profiles to be collected" (puzzle 20). JEP 483 reports a 42% faster start for its examples; JEP 515 a further 19% for one program. JDK 28, due in March 2027, is to store compiled machine code in the cache as well (JEP 544, ahead-of-time code compilation). Those JDK 24 to 28 numbers are the JEPs' own; this course ran only JDK 21.

The archive must match

It's only valid for the same JDK and a compatible class path. Run the app's archive with an extra folder in front of the class path and HotSpot quietly ignores it:

$ java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -cp extra:start.jar StartKt
[0.011s][warning][cds] shared class paths mismatch (hint: enable -Xlog:class+path=info to diagnose the failure)
[0.011s][warning][cds,dynamic] Unable to use shared archive. The top archive failed to load: app.jsa
b.dev, a.dev, c.dev

The program still runs, just without the archive. Rebuilding the jar has the same effect: in this run, touching start.jar made HotSpot print "start.jar timestamp has changed." and load Bookmark from the jar again. So recreate the archive with every build. With -Xshare:on the same mismatch is an error, and the JVM stops before main runs. JEP 310 recommends testing with on and running production with the default, auto.

The edges

  • The training run decides what's in it. JEP 483: "an AOT cache only helps insofar as the training run does similar things as production runs." Classes the training run never loaded still come from the jar.
  • A static archive, the older way. -Xshare:dump with a class list (written by a run with the DumpLoadedClassList option) writes an archive that replaces the JDK's; in this run its median was 41 and 38 ms. ArchiveClassesAtExit needs one step fewer.
  • Archives are bigger than jars. The java manual: "about 2 to 5 times larger than classes stored in JAR files". app.jsa was 1.9 megabytes here.
  • Android solves startup differently: dex2oat compiles ahead of time, and a Baseline Profile ships the profile with the app (puzzle 18).

The analogy

Every morning the office unpacks the same filing cabinets from the delivery boxes, reads each manual and puts it on the shelf in the office's own format. Class data sharing photographs the finished shelf once; the next morning the photo is pinned up and the clerks start reading it straight away. The town keeps one photo of its standard manuals for every office; an office can take its own photo of its own shelf after a normal day. The AOT cache also photographs which forms were filled in most, so the specialists can start writing sheets on day one. A photo of another office's shelf is useless, so a mismatch means unpacking boxes as usual.

Run it yourself

Save the program as Start.kt, then:

kotlinc Start.kt -include-runtime -d start.jar
java -Xlog:class+load -jar start.jar | grep -c "shared objects file"
java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -jar start.jar
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -Xlog:class+load -jar start.jar | grep "Bookmark"
time java -Xshare:off -jar start.jar
time java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -jar start.jar

Before running the last two, predict which one is faster, and by about how much. Run each several times; single timings vary.

Check yourself

You add a new class to your app and rebuild start.jar, but keep the old app.jsa. What happens at startup?

Not quite. HotSpot checks the jar's timestamp and drops the whole app archive when it changed. Re-read that part ↑

Not quite. Only -Xshare:on makes an unusable archive an error; by default the JVM continues. Re-read that part ↑

Right. A changed jar means a new training run.

Why does an app archive cut startup roughly in half here but not make main's sorting code faster?

Not quite. CDS stores parsed classes, not machine code; machine code in the cache is JEP 544, JDK 28.

Right. Classes ready is not code compiled.

Not quite. True for this tiny program, but an archive of classes never contains compiled code, whatever the program.

Your service runs in containers that start for every batch job. Which change from module 4 helps its first second most?

Not quite. JMH measures code; it doesn't change how your service starts. Re-read that part ↑

Not quite. Puzzle 23: final changes little, and only for code that is already hot. Re-read that part ↑

Right. Startup work done once ahead, not in every container.

Sources
  • JEP 310: Application Class-Data Sharing (JDK 10) ("Class-Data Sharing, introduced in JDK 5, allows a set of classes to be pre-processed into a shared archive file that can then be memory-mapped at runtime to reduce startup time."; "If the -Xshare:on option is specified, the JVM will treat this as an error condition and fail to start."; "Please note that -Xshare:auto will also disable AppCDS if there's a classpath mismatch. Therefore, we recommend that you first test with -Xshare:on to ensure there's no classpath mismatch, and then use -Xshare:auto in the production environment.")
  • JEP 341: Default CDS Archives (JDK 12) ("Enhance the JDK build process to generate a class data-sharing (CDS) archive, using the default class list, on 64-bit platforms.")
  • JEP 350: Dynamic CDS Archives (JDK 13) ("Extend application class-data sharing to allow the dynamic archiving of classes at the end of Java application execution. The archived classes will include all loaded application classes and library classes that are not present in the default, base-layer CDS archive."; "% bin/java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=hello.jsa -cp hello.jar Hello"; "% bin/java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=hello.jsa -cp hello.jar Hello")
  • JEP 483: Ahead-of-Time Class Loading & Linking (JDK 24) ("Improve startup time by making the classes of an application instantly available, in a loaded and linked state, when the HotSpot Java Virtual Machine starts."; "$ java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf"; "$ java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar"; "$ java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App ..."; "an improvement of 42%"; "Keep in mind that an AOT cache only helps insofar as the training run does similar things as production runs."; "(Update: As of JDK 27, -XX:AOTMode=on is now -XX:AOTMode=required.)")
  • JEP 514: Ahead-of-Time Command-Line Ergonomics (JDK 25) ("Make it easier to create ahead-of-time caches, which accelerate the startup of Java applications, by simplifying the commands required for common use cases."; "$ java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -cp app.jar com.example.App ...")
  • JEP 515: Ahead-of-Time Method Profiling (JDK 25) ("Improve warmup time by making method-execution profiles from a previous run of an application instantly available, when the HotSpot Java Virtual Machine starts. This will enable the JIT compiler to generate native code immediately upon application startup, rather than having to wait for profiles to be collected."; "an improvement of 19%")
  • JEP 544: Ahead-of-Time Code Compilation (Release 28) ("Improve startup and warmup time by making optimized native code for an application instantly available when the HotSpot Java Virtual Machine starts.") and JDK 28 schedule ("2027/03/09 General Availability"); status checked 22 November 2026.
  • The java command (JDK 21): Application Class Data Sharing ("Application Class Data Sharing (AppCDS) stores classes used by your applications in an archive file. Since these classes are stored in a format that can be loaded very quickly (compared to classes stored in a JAR file), AppCDS can improve the start-up time of your applications."; "This archive contains about 1300 core library classes that are used by most applications."; "Classes in the CDS archive are stored in an optimized format that's about 2 to 5 times larger than classes stored in JAR files"; "-Xshare:mode Sets the class data sharing (CDS) mode."; "on Require using shared class data, otherwise fail.")
  • The class counts, the archives, the warnings and the timings (median of 21 runs, two rounds each) were produced in this session with kotlinc 2.2.21 and OpenJDK 21.0.12. The JDK 24 to 28 features were not run here.

What you now know

Class data sharing maps an archive of already parsed classes into memory instead of reading and parsing class files: the JDK ships one for its own classes, and a training run can write one for your app. JDK 24's AOT cache also stores classes loaded and linked, JDK 25 adds method profiles, and the archive is only used if the class path and JDK match the training run.
